summary: The Netherlands is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (with the ETIAS travel authorization being phased in), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa costing €90. Long stays require an MVV entry visa and an IND residence permit.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since June 11, 2024.

Approximate; updated annually. The host university applies to the IND on the student's behalf as a recognized sponsor.
Approximate; updated annually. One-year permit to look for work after graduating from a Dutch university or a top-200 world university (apply within 3 years of graduation).

visaTypes.name: Work Permit (Single Permit / Highly Skilled Migrant)

fee.notes: Approximate; updated annually. The employer, usually an IND-recognized sponsor, files the application; highly skilled migrants must meet a salary threshold.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

proofOfFunds.text: The Netherlands expects non-EU visitors to show around €55 per person per day for the length of the stay (cash, cards or bank statements).

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border. There is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Debit cards and contactless are the norm. Many supermarkets and shops are card/PIN-only and do not accept cash at all, and some take only debit cards, not credit cards, so carry a debit card as backup.

safety.text: The Netherlands is a very safe destination. The main visitor risks are pickpocketing in central Amsterdam and on trains, and bicycle theft.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Netherlands Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: April–May for tulip season and King's Day, June–September for the warmest weather; pack for rain in any month.

idp.text: Netherlands is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: Netherlands is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Netherlands yet.

tips.text: The 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just the Netherlands — days spent in Belgium or Germany count against the same allowance.
Never walk or stand in the red-paved bike lanes — cyclists have priority, move fast and will not stop. Look both ways for bikes before crossing any street.
Public transport uses OVpay: check in and out with a contactless bank card or phone on every train, tram, metro and bus — forgetting to check out triggers a penalty fare.
Don't rely on cash: many Dutch supermarkets and shops are card-only, and some accept only debit (Maestro/V PAY) rather than foreign credit cards.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for the Netherlands?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit the Netherlands and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorization (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does a Netherlands Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries.

faq.question: How do I stay in the Netherlands longer than 90 days?
faq.answer: Most non-EU nationals need an MVV long-stay entry visa combined with an IND residence permit, applied for in a single procedure (TEV), usually via a Dutch sponsor such as an employer or university. Fees are roughly €200–€400 depending on the permit type and are updated annually. Check ind.nl.

faq.question: What is the Dutch orientation year (zoekjaar) permit?
faq.answer: Graduates of Dutch universities or top-200 world universities can apply within 3 years of graduating for a one-year residence permit to look for work in the Netherlands, with unrestricted labor-market access. The fee is around €243 (updated annually).

faq.question: Is cash widely accepted in the Netherlands?
faq.answer: Less than you might expect: many supermarkets, shops and even market stalls are card-only, and some accept only debit cards. Carry a contactless debit card; a small amount of cash is still useful for markets and tips.
